newsitem.title: USA: Ford posts record profits of $2.53 billion.
newsitem.headline: Ford posts record profits of $2.53 billion.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. posted record profits of $2.53 billion for the second quarter Wednesday, but investors, worried the company's stock rise has peaked, responded by knocking the stock lower.

Ford's earnings jumped 33 percent, making it the best quarter ever among Detroit's Big Three. Ford earned $2.06 on a per-share basis. A year ago, Ford posted profits of $1.90 billion, or $1.56 a share.
Ford's stock, one of the most active on the New York Stock Exchange, fell $1.625 to $40.50 in afternoon trading. The stock has increased about 31 percent since the beginning of the year.
"You've had a great run," said Paine Webber analyst Michael Ward, who downgraded his recommendation on the stock to "neutral" from "attractive."
Ward said he took the action because Ford has largely worked through its most recent wave of new product introductions, which drives earnings growth.
"We just happen to think Chrysler, with the launch of the LH cars and the Durango, has a better chance for earnings acceleration," he said.

Relying on cost-cutting and new products, Ford officials insisted they can continue to produce healthy financial results despite increasingly intense market conditions in the United States and abroad.
"I don't buy at all that this is the top and this is the time to say it's over," said Ford Chief Financial Officer John Devine.

Ford's results included a gain of $100 million, reflecting a gain from the initial public offering of Hertz Corp. and a charge for closing several plants, as well as the sale of Ford's heavy truck business to Freightliner.

The No. 2 automaker credited its performance to $1 billion in lower costs and the introduction of several new cars and trucks. Ford has now cut $1.8 billion in costs in the first half, and Devine said the company hopes to bring its total 1997 cost cuts to more than $2 billion.

Net income from Ford's worldwide automotive operations rose to $1.74 billion from $1.10 billion. The increase reflected strong profits in Ford's core U.S. automotive operations, which nearly doubled to $1.19 billion from $697 million.
Worldwide sales and revenues were $40.3 billion, compared with $39 billion a year earlier. Ford had worldwide vehicle unit shipments of 1,879,000, a 3.8 percent increase from 1,810,000 a year ago.

Devine sounded several notes of caution during a briefing with reporters at Ford's corporate headquarters. Ford still has work to do in its worldwide cost-cutting initiative. Ford's European profits fell to $157 million in the second quarter from $196 million a year ago, and it expects to break even in Europe for the full year.

Ford's Financial Services Group, a huge profit performer a year ago, had flat income of $795 million for the second quarter. Devine said second-half profits at Ford Credit, the largest part of the financial services unit, will continue to be under pressure from higher depreciation costs on leased vehicles. Ford Credit posted second-quarter net income of $279 million, down from $376 million.
The second half of 1997 will also be marked by more intense competitive market conditions in the United States what will put continued pressure on marketing costs, Devine said.
"We're going to see -- really -- wars in every part of the segments," he said.
